# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
trail resume: JSON action report and idempotency guarantee

--json was only legal with --no-resume, so an agent that actually
performed a resume had no structured result. --json now composes with
the act path and emits a compact action report: trail identity, actions
taken (fetched/switched branch, checkpoint id, commits the checkpoint is
behind HEAD), restored sessions, and a continuation whose agent and
session id are separate fields so headless orchestrators can construct
their own invocation instead of unquoting a command string.

Failure contract: typed resume errors (worktree_clash with the other
worktree's path, no_checkpoint, metadata_unavailable) emit the report
with an error object on stdout and exit non-zero; pre-action failures
(auth, validation, assertions, uncommitted changes) keep the default
empty-stdout/stderr-text behavior, so callers parse stdout only when it
is non-empty. --no-resume --json keeps the inspection payload unchanged.

Re-running resume is pinned as an idempotent success by an integration
test: agents retry, and the second run must keep the restored log.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -4

`entire trail resume` was designed interactive-first; for agent callers (the most common caller) the non-interactive path was never finished. This PR completes it without touching the core semantics — checkpoint discovery, restore, and interactive launch all stay as they are.

## What changed

**Never block, never need `--force` to complete.** The older-checkpoint confirmation (`promptResumeFromOlderCheckpoint`) fired without a `CanPromptInteractively()` guard, so any branch with commits newer than its last checkpoint hard-failed non-interactive runs — teaching agents to always pass `--force`, a flag that also overwrites local session logs. Non-interactive runs now proceed from the latest checkpoint with a one-line notice; `--force` regains its single meaning.

**Honest exit codes.** Every "nothing was resumed" path exited 0: the worktree clash, the no-checkpoint branch, and three metadata-unavailable paths in `checkRemoteMetadata`. All now return errors. Interactive user declines remain exit 0 by design (unreachable for agents).

**Typed errors.** `ResumeWorktreeClashError` (carries the other worktree's path), `ResumeNoCheckpointError`, `ResumeMetadataUnavailableError` — recoverable via `errors.As` through `SilentError`, so orchestrators can act on failures instead of parsing stderr.

**Slim act path.** Actually resuming no longer prints the trail header, session table, findings tables, and command menu (that's `trail show`/`trail finding`'s job — and the act path skips those fetches entirely). Output is now: identity line, actions taken, and the default session's resume command as the final stdout line, machine-liftable. `--no-resume` keeps the full inspection dump.

**`--json` action report.** `--json` now composes with real resumes: trail, actions (fetched/switched, checkpoint id, commits behind HEAD), restored sessions, and a structured continuation (`agent` + `session_id` as fields). Typed failures emit the report with an `error` object and exit non-zero; pre-action failures keep empty stdout + stderr text. `--no-resume --json` is unchanged.

**Idempotency pinned.** Agents retry; a repeated resume is a clean no-op success, now guarded by an integration test.

`entire session resume` shares the restore engine and picks up the prompt guard and exit-code fixes; its tests are updated accordingly.

Companion PR (independent, also off main): trail show --json.

## Testing

- Unit (7277), integration (380), and full Vogon canary all green
- New unit tests pin the prompt-guard notice, typed-error round-trips, worktree-clash error, slim-output contract, and JSON report shape
- Updated integration + e2e tests that previously pinned exit-0-on-nothing-resumed

The whole change is deletion-shaped where it matters: no restore logic was touched. The act path got *smaller* (fetches removed, output removed) while the contract got stronger (typed errors, exit codes) — which is why every interactive behavior could stay byte-identical except the slimmer preamble.

All three threads are resolved. Summary:

## PR A (#1884) — findings fixed, pushed as `863befdf87`

Both findings were legitimate bugs in my `--json` path:
1. **Prompt could still fire under `--json` at a real terminal** — the older-checkpoint guard checked terminal interactivity, not JSON mode. Fixed by giving `restoreFromCurrentBranch` an `allowPrompts` parameter the JSON driver sets to false — deliberately decoupled from `--force` so the log-overwrite semantics stay untouched.
2. **Bogus `--session <id>` with `--json` silently continued a different session with exit 0** — now fails with the same "not found in the restored checkpoint" error as the human path.

GitHub CI on PR A is green; the Entire gate will re-review the new code version. On size: 1045/90 across 12 files — about two-thirds tests, inside my 800–1400 estimate but at the top of it, and the prod side grew more than my "mostly deletion" framing suggested. Fair criticism.

## PR B (#1885) — not guilty; main is broken

The failing test fails on pristine `main` with PR B's diff stashed (verified locally before the PR, now confirmed in CI). Root cause: a **semantic conflict between #1824 and #1811** — #1811 routes `explain --generate` summary writes through the git-refs store, whose local miss triggers #1824's fetch probe; in a repo with *no remotes at all*, the probe runs `git ls-remote origin`, gets exit 128, and the "transport failure is never absence" contract turns a remoteless repo into a hard error. Each PR was green against pre-merge main.

## PR C (#1886) — the main fix, opened

New branch off main: a narrow guard in `FetchCheckpointRef` — no checkpoint_remote configured + no origin remote = no remote that could host checkpoint refs, so local absence is the verdict. The two existing contract protections (unresolvable-checkpoint-remote refusal, transport-failure-never-absence) are untouched and their tests still pass; the broken explain test goes green. Full unit suite (8475 tests) passes.

Once #1886 merges, re-running PR B's checks should clear it without touching the branch.

content.text:
Because it fixes `main`, not PR B — and bundling it would have misfiled it in three ways:

1. **Ownership of the breakage.** The bug is an interaction between #1824 and #1811 — two merges that have nothing to do with `trail show --json`. If the fix rode inside PR B, the repair for "main's backfill probe breaks fully local repos" would be hidden in a PR titled "trail show: add --json", invisible to the people who should review it — the #1824/#1811 authors, who own that probe's absence-vs-failure contract and might prefer a different fix (or a revert). As its own PR, it's reviewable by the right eyes on its own merits.

2. **Everyone is blocked, not just PR B.** Main's tip fails `test-core` for *any* branch that includes it — PR A will hit the same wall the moment main gets merged into it, and so will every other PR opened today. The fix has to land on main to help anyone; inside PR B it only helps PR B, and only when PR B merges.

3. **Unblocking without coupling.** With the fix separate, the merge order is clean: #1886 lands, PR B's checks re-run green with zero changes to its branch. If they were bundled, PR B's two-line flag addition couldn't merge until reviewers were satisfied with checkpoint-probe semantics — the trivial change held hostage by the subtle one. That's the same "don't crowd the verb" logic as the rest of this work, applied to PRs.

It also matches your standing constraint — independent branches off main, nothing stacked: #1886 is off main, and neither A nor B depends on its *branch*, only on it reaching main.

The trade-off I accepted: three open PRs instead of two, and PR B stays red until #1886 merges. If you'd rather collapse it, the realistic alternative wasn't "fold into B" but "close B and re-open it after main is fixed" — more churn for the same result.

content.text:
The failing test does this: in a throwaway git repo (**with no remotes — no origin, nothing**), run `entire explain --generate` and check the summary gets saved.

The save path goes like this on current main:

1. To save the summary, the code first asks: "does this checkpoint live in the new refs-based storage?"
2. The local ref isn't there, so — this is #1824's change — before concluding "not here," it tries to **fetch the ref from the remote**, to be safe.
3. It runs `git ls-remote origin`… but the repo **has no origin**. Git errors out ("'origin' does not appear to be a git repository").
4. The code treats any fetch error as "network problem — I can't tell whether the checkpoint exists remotely," and refuses to guess. The save aborts with that error.
5. Test fails: the summary never got saved.

The bug is step 4's logic applied to step 3's situation: "I couldn't reach the remote" is the wrong conclusion when **there is no remote**. A repo with zero remotes can't have the checkpoint stored remotely anywhere — there's nothing to be cautious about.

#1886 adds one check before step 3: *if the repo has no origin and no configured checkpoint remote, don't attempt a fetch — just answer "not here."* With that answer, the save routine moves on to where the checkpoint actually lives (the v1 branch), writes the summary there, and the test passes.

Dug into the actual routing code (`routing_store.go` from #1811). Short answers:

**Why does saving probe the remote at all?** Deliberate, from #1824. Scenario it protects: you made a checkpoint on machine A (stored as a git ref, pushed), now machine B generates a summary. B doesn't have the ref locally. Without the fetch-probe, B would conclude "not in the refs store," fall back, and write the summary to the old v1 branch — while the checkpoint actually lives in refs. Data forked. So before trusting "absent," it fetch-checks the remote.

**Is "check the v1 branch first on writes" better?** No — a checkpoint can exist in *both* stores (migration), and reads prefer refs. Writes must follow the same priority or the summary lands where reads won't look first. So the probe order is right; the only broken case is "there is no remote to check" — which is exactly what #1886 special-cases.

**And I found the smoking gun for why this slipped through:** #1811's own code comment says backfill probes are "local-only … does not on-demand fetch." That was true when written — but #1824 (merged two hours *earlier*, into which #1811 never merged) is precisely the PR that made backfill probes fetch. The two PRs have contradictory designs for the same probe and were never run together until main. So #1886 isn't patching intended breakage — it's reconciling two intents: keep #1824's fetch-check when a remote exists, skip it when none exists. Worth pointing victor (and #1824's author) at that stale comment when they review #1886.

AUTHOR: peyton-alt
TITLE: fix(checkpoint): fetch a locally-missing ref before declaring a backfill target absent

Follow-up to the #1811 review (addressed directly per discussion, no issue filed). Complete fix: store-layer semantics **and** production wiring.

## Problem

The git-refs store's **reads** on-demand fetch a checkpoint ref that's missing locally; its **backfill writes** (summary, stop-time transcript finalize, attribution) probed with a local-only lookup. For a checkpoint written or migrated on another machine, a backfill declared it absent — landing on a stale fallback copy under kind routing (#1811), or failing — while reads served the refs copy, leaving the backfilled data permanently invisible.

## Fix (three layers)

**1. Store: backfills fetch-probe** — `refBaseForBackfill` → `resolveRefMaybeFetch` fetches a locally-missing ref once when a fetcher is wired. Creates keep the local-only probe (their ref never exists yet). Zero cost when the ref exists locally (pinned).

**2. Absence ≠ failure at the fetch layer** — `remote.FetchCheckpointRef` (moved from the cli package so strategy hooks can import it; thin aliases keep old call sites) now probes with `ls-remote` before fetching: a ref the remote genuinely lacks returns an error wrapping `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound` → classified as absence → safe fallthrough under kind routing. Transport failures on either leg surface as-is — never absence, so a dead network can't fork a write onto a stale copy. This was the blocker that made naive wiring unsafe (`git fetch` of a missing refspec fails like a network error).

**3. Wiring with a hook-safe budget** — `remote.BoundedCheckpointRefFetcher(remote.WriteProbeFetchBudget)` (15s per probe) wired at the three backfill write sites: explain `--generate`'s write store, the stop-hook transcript finalize, and post-commit attribution. The git-refs store memoizes the first transport-level fetch failure per store instance, so a stop hook finalizing N checkpoints on a dead network pays the outage once, briefly. Remote absence is per-ref and never memoized.

## Verification

- TDD throughout: store-level fetch-restores-ref (all three backfill types, with read-back + parent-hash assertions), fetch-failure-aborts (`NotErrorIs ErrCheckpointNotFound`), absent-after-fetch, local-ref-never-fetches, creates-never-fetch, absence-classification chain-through, and failure-memo behavior (transport memoized once; absence never)
- Remote-level fixtures against a local bare origin: missing ref → absence sentinel; present ref → fetched into the local ref; unreachable remote → hard error
- Multi-agent review pass applied (comments re-anchored order-agnostically vs #1811; `FetchCheckpointRef`'s inverted contract comment fixed; `ref-checkpoint-backend.md` updated)
- Full unit suite green (8180 tests), `mise run fmt` + `mise run lint` clean

## Relationship to #1811

Independent; merges in either order (comments phrased order-agnostically). Reconciliation: whichever lands second drops #1811's "backfill absence probes are local-only" sentence from the kindRoutingStore `Write` doc comment.

Absence ≠ failure at the fetch layer** — `remote.FetchCheckpointRef` (moved from the cli package so strategy hooks can import it; thin aliases keep old call sites) now probes with `ls-remote` before fetching: a ref the remote genuinely lacks returns an error wrapping `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound` → classified as absence → safe fallthrough under kind routing. Transport failures on either leg surface as-is — never absence, so a dead network can't fork a write onto a stale copy. This was the blocker that made naive wiring unsafe (`git fetch` of a missing refspec fails like a network error).

**3. Wiring with a hook-safe budget** — `remote.BoundedCheckpointRefFetcher(remote.WriteProbeFetchBudget)` (15s per probe) wired at the three backfill write sites: explain `--generate`'s write store, the stop-hook transcript finalize, and post-commit attribution. The git-refs store memoizes the first transport-level fetch failure per store instance, so a stop hook finalizing N checkpoints on a dead network pays the outage once, briefly. Remote absence is per-ref and never memoized.

## Verification

- TDD throughout: store-level fetch-restores-ref (all three backfill types, with read-back + parent-hash assertions), fetch-failure-aborts (`NotErrorIs ErrCheckpointNotFound`), absent-after-fetch, local-ref-never-fetches, creates-never-fetch, absence-classification chain-through, and failure-memo behavior (transport memoized once; absence never)
- Remote-level fixtures against a local bare origin: missing ref → absence sentinel; present ref → fetched into the local ref; unreachable remote → hard error
- Multi-agent review pass applied (comments re-anchored order-agnostically vs #1811; `FetchCheckpointRef`'s inverted contract comment fixed; `ref-checkpoint-backend.md` updated)
- Full unit suite green (8180 tests), `mise run fmt` + `mise run lint` clean

## Relationship to #1811

Independent; merges in either order (comments phrased order-agnostically). Reconciliation: whichever lands second drops #1811's "backfill absence probes are local-only" sentence from the kindRoutingStore `Write` doc comment.

AUTHOR: peyton-alt  TITLE: fix(checkpoint): kind-route backfill writes to the store holding the checkpoint
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/905
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`entire checkpoint explain --generate <hex-id>` under a git-refs primary generated the AI summary, then **discarded it**, and printed the misleading error `no checkpoint or commit found matching "<id>"` — for a checkpoint the same command had just displayed.

Root cause: `kindRoutingStore` kind-routes **reads** across both git backends (a hex ID under a git-refs primary reads refs, then falls back to the v1 branch), but **writes** always went to the configured primary. A pre-migration hex checkpoint that only exists on the v1 branch therefore resolved on read but failed every backfill with `ErrCheckpointNotFound` from the refs store.

## Fix

Backfill writes (`SessionSummary`, `SessionTranscript`, `CheckpointAttribution`) target an *existing* checkpoint, so they now follow the same store order reads use, falling through to the next store on `ErrCheckpointNotFound`:

- hex under git-refs primary → refs (via the mirror fan-out writer), then v1 branch
- ULID → always refs, regardless of primary
- a backfill landing on the primary still fans out to mirrors; one landing on a fallback store skips them (mirrors follow the primary)
- creates (`Session`) are unchanged — their ID is minted to match the primary's format

## Verification

- TDD: new `TestKindRoutingStore_*` tests written first (bug repro fails with `checkpoint not found` before the fix)
- Full unit suite green (8122 tests), `mise run fmt` + `mise run lint` clean
- Verified end-to-end against the real repro: `entire checkpoint explain --generate 2cb795c79075` in this repo now persists the summary to the v1 branch and it reads back

Related follow-ups shipped separately (not stacked): explain's misleading error-message conflation, and the stale `entire explain --generate` hint text.

All trail-review findings across the three trails are now addressed and pushed:

**Trail 961 / PR #1884** — of the 5 findings, 3 were already stale (my earlier fixes for session-not-found routing, the TTY prompt, and the silent `--session` fallback). The 2 current ones are fixed in `1c624c1505`:
- `checkpoint_behind_head` was computed from the branch's *latest* checkpoint even when `--checkpoint`/`--session` resumed an older one — it's now only reported on the default latest path where it's truthful.
- A checkpoint whose restore yields zero sessions (log content unavailable) produced a success report with exit 0. Now a typed `no_sessions_restored` failure — on both the JSON path and the human non-interactive path, since the help text promises it for both; interactive zero still exits 0 because that's a user declining a prompt.

**Trail 962 / PR #1885** — fixed in `fc80495593`: the JSON payload serialized "description fetch failed" and "description genuinely empty" identically as `""`. It now carries `description_loaded`, mirroring the distinction the text path already draws.

**Trail 963 / PR #1886** — fixed in `cdd98e4abd`: a present-but-malformed `checkpoint_remote` (which `GetCheckpointRemote` collapses to nil) no longer counts as "not configured" — the absence shortcut requires the key to be absent entirely, so a botched config stays a hard failure. New regression test for exactly that shape.

Each fix went in test-first where the seam allowed, and each branch re-ran its gate (fmt, lint, unit; plus integration + canary on trail-resume) before pushing. The gates and bots will re-review the new commits; the stale 961 findings should resolve on re-review since the code they point at has changed.

# Comprehensive PR Review

Run a comprehensive pull request review using multiple specialized agents, each focusing on a different aspect of code quality.

**Review Aspects (optional):** "1886"

## Review Workflow:

1. **Determine Review Scope**
   - Check git status to identify changed files
   - Parse arguments to see if user requested specific review aspects
   - Default: Run all applicable reviews

2. **Available Review Aspects:**

   - **comments** - Analyze code comment accuracy and maintainability
   - **tests** - Review test coverage quality and completeness
   - **errors** - Check error handling for silent failures
   - **types** - Analyze type design and invariants (if new types added)
   - **code** - General code review for project guidelines
   - **simplify** - Simplify code for clarity and maintainability
   - **all** - Run all applicable reviews (default)

3. **Identify Changed Files**
   - Run `git diff --name-only` to see modified files
   - Check if PR already exists: `gh pr view`
   - Identify file types and what reviews apply

4. **Determine Applicable Reviews**

   Based on changes:
   - **Always applicable**: code-reviewer (general quality)
   - **If test files changed**: pr-test-analyzer
   - **If comments/docs added**: comment-analyzer
   - **If error handling changed**: silent-failure-hunter
   - **If types added/modified**: type-design-analyzer
   - **After passing review**: code-simplifier (polish and refine)

5. **Launch Review Agents**

   **Sequential approach** (one at a time):
   - Easier to understand and act on
   - Each report is complete before next
   - Good for interactive review

   **Parallel approach** (user can request):
   - Launch all agents simultaneously
   - Faster for comprehensive review
   - Results come back together

6. **Aggregate Results**

   After agents complete, summarize:
   - **Critical Issues** (must fix before merge)
   - **Important Issues** (should fix)
   - **Suggestions** (nice to have)
   - **Positive Observations** (what's good)

7. **Provide Action Plan**

   Organize findings:
   ```markdown
   # PR Review Summary

   ## Critical Issues (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Issue description [file:line]

   ## Important Issues (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Issue description [file:line]

   ## Suggestions (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Suggestion [file:line]

   ## Strengths
   - What's well-done in this PR

   ## Recommended Action
   1. Fix critical issues first
   2. Address important issues
   3. Consider suggestions
   4. Re-run review after fixes
   ```

## Usage Examples:

**Full review (default):**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr
```

**Specific aspects:**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr tests errors
# Reviews only test coverage and error handling

/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr comments
# Reviews only code comments

/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr simplify
# Simplifies code after passing review
```

**Parallel review:**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr all parallel
# Launches all agents in parallel
```

## Agent Descriptions:

**comment-analyzer**:
- Verifies comment accuracy vs code
- Identifies comment rot
- Checks documentation completeness

**pr-test-analyzer**:
- Reviews behavioral test coverage
- Identifies critical gaps
- Evaluates test quality

**silent-failure-hunter**:
- Finds silent failures
- Reviews catch blocks
- Checks error logging

**type-design-analyzer**:
- Analyzes type encapsulation
- Reviews invariant expression
- Rates type design quality

**code-reviewer**:
- Checks CLAUDE.md compliance
- Detects bugs and issues
- Reviews general code quality

**code-simplifier**:
- Simplifies complex code
- Improves clarity and readability
- Applies project standards
- Preserves functionality

## Tips:

- **Run early**: Before creating PR, not after
- **Focus on changes**: Agents analyze git diff by default
- **Address critical first**: Fix high-priority issues before lower priority
- **Re-run after fixes**: Verify issues are resolved
- **Use specific reviews**: Target specific aspects when you know the concern

## Workflow Integration:

**Before committing:**
```
1. Write code
2. Run: /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr code errors
3. Fix any critical issues
4. Commit
```

**Before creating PR:**
```
1. Stage all changes
2. Run: /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr all
3. Address all critical and important issues
4. Run specific reviews again to verify
5. Create PR
```

**After PR feedback:**
```
1. Make requested changes
2. Run targeted reviews based on feedback
3. Verify issues are resolved
4. Push updates
```

## Notes:

- Agents run autonomously and return detailed reports
- Each agent focuses on its specialty for deep analysis
- Results are actionable with specific file:line references
- Agents use appropriate models for their complexity
- All agents available in `/agents` list

# Review: PR #1886 — remote: classify a remoteless repo as checkpoint-ref absence, not outage

**Scope:** 2 files, +103/-0. `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/remote/checkpoint_ref.go` (guard + helper) and its test file. Base `main`, head `fix/local-repo-checkpoint-probe` (verified this worktree is on that branch).

## Overview

Main is red from a semantic conflict between #1824 (fetch-probe: transport failure is never absence) and #1811 (backfill writes routed through the refs store). In a repo with no remotes, `FetchCheckpointRef`'s origin-name fallback runs `git ls-remote origin`, gets exit 128, and the contract turns "no remotes exist" into a hard error, breaking backfill routing and `explain --generate`. The fix inserts a pre-probe guard: when the fetch target is the non-authoritative `"origin"` name fallback, settings load successfully, no `checkpoint_remote` key exists at all, and origin has no URL, return `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound` (absence) without probing. Three regression tests cover the matrix.

## Correctness analysis

**Does the guard preserve the false-absence protections? Largely yes.** I traced every path into the `("origin", false)` fallback of `checkpointFetchTarget` (util.go:41-47, reached only when `fetchURLAuthoritative` errors or yields an empty URL — which always implies origin's URL was unresolvable):

- Unreadable settings → `loadErr != nil` → guard skipped → hard failure (test 2 verifies).
- Key present but malformed (`GetCheckpointRemote` collapses to nil, settings.go:1421-1432) → `checkpointRemoteKeyPresent` true → guard skipped → hard failure (test 3 verifies). This correctly distinguishes "no intent" from "botched intent", which `GetCheckpointRemote` alone cannot.
- Valid `checkpoint_remote` + no origin → key present → guard skipped → hard failure. Correct.
- The fallback-emptiness refusal (checkpoint_ref.go:97-104) and the unreachable-remote path are untouched.
- The guard cannot fire on a resolved-URL target: `fetchTarget == originRemote` only matches the literal name fallback (a real remote URL never equals `"origin"`).

**Important — canceled/expired context is misclassified as absence** (checkpoint_ref.go:84). `GetRemoteURL` → `gitremote.GetRemoteURLInDir` (gitremote.go:98-108) runs `git remote get-url` via `exec.CommandContext` and collapses **every** failure — including context cancellation — into `"remote %q not found"`. Walkthrough: parent ctx already canceled → `fetchURLAuthoritative`'s own `getRemoteURL` fails → `originURL == ""` → (settings load ignores ctx, succeeds; no key) → falls back to `("origin", false)` → guard: load OK, key absent, `GetRemoteURL` fails again → returns `ErrReferenceNotFound` — **false absence in a repo that has an origin remote**. The refs store then acts on it (refs_store.go:396-402) and write routing falls through to another backend — exactly the misdirection #1824's contract exists to prevent. Note the surrounding code is deliberately careful about this same class: refs_store.go:404-407 refuses to memoize ctx-cancellation failures. How realistic: `HookCheckpointRefFetcher`/`BoundedCheckpointRefFetcher` mint fresh 15s child timeouts, so it needs the *parent* hook ctx to be dead (overall hook deadline exhausted mid-loop, SIGINT) — an edge, but a one-line fix closes it:

```go
if _, urlErr := GetRemoteURL(ctx, originRemote); urlErr != nil && ctx.Err() == nil {
```

(Other exec-failure modes — git binary missing, unreadable repo — also collapse into `urlErr != nil`, but in those worlds the subsequent ls-remote fails everywhere anyway; ctx is the only one where the guard flips an otherwise-correct outcome.)

**TOCTOU between the guard's re-resolution and `checkpointFetchTarget` — analyzed, safe.** The guard re-runs `settings.Load` and `git remote get-url` that `fetchURLAuthoritative` just ran. I checked all four drift orderings: remote added between calls → guard doesn't fire, proceeds to a now-valid probe (safe); key added → guard skipped, hard failure (safe); key removed → absence matches final state; remote removed → can't matter (fallback already implied it was gone). No dangerous ordering, so this is a cleanliness concern, not correctness (see suggestions).

**Transient `GetRemoteURL` failure while origin exists:** to even reach the guard, the *first* `getRemoteURL` inside `fetchURLAuthoritative` must already have failed, so a single transient blip doesn't get you there — it takes two consecutive failures with the same ctx. Outside the ctx-cancellation case above (where both fail deterministically), there is no plausible transient double-failure on a local `git remote get-url`; acceptable.

## Project conventions

**Important — settings access convention** (checkpoint_ref.go:131-137). `checkpointRemoteKeyPresent` reaches into `s.StrategyOptions["checkpoint_remote"]` from the `remote` package, duplicating the storage-key literal that lives in settings.go:1417. CLAUDE.md is explicit: "Do NOT ... create new settings helpers without adding them to the `settings` package." This helper is a settings helper by function; it belongs next to `GetCheckpointRemote` as e.g. `(s *EntireSettings) CheckpointRemoteKeyPresent() bool`, keeping key-name knowledge in one file. As written, a future key rename would silently break this guard.

Otherwise clean: tests use `testutil.InitRepo` per convention; no `t.Parallel()` is correct here since every test calls `t.Chdir` (documented exception); error wrapping uses the sentinel properly; comments explain the *why* at appropriate length.

## Performance (git hooks, 15s budget)

Net positive. The guard's cost is one string compare on the happy path (resolved URL → skipped entirely). On the fallback path it adds one `settings.Load` (local file reads) + one `git remote get-url` subprocess, and in the remoteless case it *removes* the doomed `git ls-remote origin` subprocess. Both added operations are local and fast (~10ms). The per-store failure memo in the refs store is unaffected — absence is per-ref and unmemoized, which is correct since remoteless-repo "absence" is cheap to recompute. Suggestion: the duplicate `settings.Load`/`get-url` could be eliminated by having `fetchURLAuthoritative` surface a "no remotes at all" signal (sentinel error or reason enum) instead of the guard re-deriving it — also removes the drift surface.

## Test coverage

Good on the stated matrix; three targeted tests with clear rationale comments:

- remoteless repo → absence (the regression)
- corrupt settings → never absence
- malformed `checkpoint_remote` → never absence

Plus verified: the four pre-existing contract tests still pass, and the red-on-main explain test passes with this fix.

Gaps (suggestion):
- **No test for the ctx-cancellation path** — a test passing an already-canceled context in a repo *with* an origin would fail today per the Important issue above, and would pin the fix.
- No test for *valid* `checkpoint_remote` + no origin; the key-present branch covers it identically to the malformed case, so this is minor.
- `"checkpoint_remote": null` — key present with nil value → treated as configured → hard failure. That's the conservative direction (safe), but worth a line in the helper's comment.

## Risk assessment

Low. The change is additive, fires only on the origin-name fallback (which always implies origin was unresolvable), and every guard-skip path degrades to today's behavior (hard failure). The one genuine contract hole is the ctx-cancellation edge; it is narrow and one line to close.

## Issue summary

| Severity | Location | Issue |
|---|---|---|
| Important | checkpoint_ref.go:84 | Canceled/expired ctx makes `GetRemoteURL` fail → false absence in a repo that has an origin; add `&& ctx.Err() == nil` |
| Important | checkpoint_ref.go:131-137 | Settings-key helper lives outside the settings package, duplicating the `"checkpoint_remote"` literal (settings.go:1417); move onto `EntireSettings` per CLAUDE.md |
| Suggestion | checkpoint_ref.go:82-88 | Guard re-derives what `fetchURLAuthoritative` already computed; surface a "no remotes" signal from resolution instead |
| Suggestion | checkpoint_ref_test.go | Add a canceled-context regression test (would catch the Important issue); optionally valid-remote+no-origin |

Verdict: approve with the ctx-cancellation guard fixed (one line) — the helper relocation can land in this PR or immediately after, given main is red and this unblocks it.

# Test Coverage Analysis — PR #1886 (remoteless-repo probe guard)

Analyzed at `/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/fix-local-probe` (branch `fix/local-repo-checkpoint-probe`, matching the PR head). Files: `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/remote/checkpoint_ref.go` and `checkpoint_ref_test.go`. All 7 tests pass. I additionally ran three hand-mutations of the guard to verify which tests pin which condition (worktree restored afterwards).

## Summary

Coverage is strong. The three new tests are behavioral, pinned at the right seam (the public `FetchCheckpointRef` error-classification contract via `ErrorIs`/`NotErrorIs plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound` — exactly what store probes consume), and two of the guard's three conditions are mutation-verified as pinned. The third condition (`GetRemoteURL(origin)` re-check) is not pinned, but analysis shows it is an equivalent mutant — unreachable-false through the public API. One genuine untested edge exists: a repo whose only remote is non-origin silently changed classification from failure to absence.

## Guard conditions — pinned or not (mutation-verified)

1. **`loadErr == nil` (unreadable settings never classify absence)** — PINNED. Mutation (guard fires on load error) → `UnreadableSettingsNeverClassifiesAbsence` fails.
2. **`!checkpointRemoteKeyPresent(s)` (present-but-malformed key blocks the shortcut)** — PINNED. Mutation (key lookup broken) → `MalformedCheckpointRemoteNeverClassifiesAbsence` fails. Note this test is load-bearing beyond the obvious: `GetCheckpointRemote()` collapses malformed→nil, so only the raw-key check distinguishes this case, and only this test guards that distinction.
3. **`GetRemoteURL(ctx, originRemote)` failing** — NOT pinned (mutation replacing it with `if true` survives the full suite). However, it's provably redundant today: `fetchURLAuthoritative` (`util.go:54-144`) only ever falls back to the literal name `"origin"` when `originURL == ""`, i.e. when `GetRemoteURL(origin)` just failed. Every reachable path into the guard already has no origin. The check is defense-in-depth against future drift in `fetchURLAuthoritative`, and is untestable through the public API without injection. **Severity 2 — acceptable as-is**; the code comment covers the intent. (Same is true of `!authoritative`: the literal-`"origin"` target is never returned as authoritative.)

The guard-must-not-fire-when-origin-exists direction is pinned by the pre-existing `PresentRefFetches` (an over-eager guard would return absence instead of fetching) and `RemoteMissingRefIsAbsence`.

## Missing edge cases

- **Severity 6 — repo whose only remote is non-origin (e.g. `git clone -o upstream`), no checkpoint_remote.** Untested, and it's the one input class where this PR genuinely changed behavior beyond the remoteless case: before, `ls-remote origin` failed with exit 128 (failure, backfill retries); now the guard classifies ABSENCE (`GetRemoteURL(origin)` fails, key absent). This is not obviously wrong — the fetch universe is only origin/checkpoint_remote — but the push side is not so restricted: `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` (`cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:326`) pushes checkpoint refs toward whatever remote the pre-push hook fires for, so refs can exist on a non-origin remote the probe will now call "absent", and absence is a signal write routing acts on. Also, the error message "repository has no remote to fetch from" is inaccurate for this repo. A test should pin whichever semantics is intended (`git remote add upstream <bare>` and assert the chosen classification); right now the decision is implicit and undocumented.
- **Severity 3 — well-formed `checkpoint_remote` + no origin.** Follows the identical guard branch as the Malformed test (`checkpointRemoteKeyPresent` is value-blind), so today it adds little. Its value would be pinning the outcome if `fetchURLAuthoritative` ever learns to resolve provider-canonical URLs without an origin (currently `util.go:120` bails before `resolveProviderCheckpointURL` when origin is missing). Optional.
- **Severity 2 — hermeticity nit:** the tests inherit `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` from the environment; a set token routes `fetchURLAuthoritative` through the token path. Tracing shows all three tests still land on the same fallback, so it can't flip results today, but a `t.Setenv("ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN", "")` would make that a non-question. Pre-existing tests share this nit.
- **Covered, no gap:** "origin exists, checkpoint_remote key absent — normal path must still probe" — the pre-existing fixture writes no settings file, so `RemoteMissingRefIsAbsence`/`PresentRefFetches` are exactly this case (they resolve origin's URL as authoritative and probe it). "Configured checkpoint_remote with origin present" stays on the fallback-emptiness refusal, pinned by `FallbackTargetNeverClassifiesAbsence`.

## Test quality

## Summary

Coverage is strong. The three new tests are behavioral, pinned at the right seam (the public `FetchCheckpointRef` error-classification contract via `ErrorIs`/`NotErrorIs plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound` — exactly what store probes consume), and two of the guard's three conditions are mutation-verified as pinned. The third condition (`GetRemoteURL(origin)` re-check) is not pinned, but analysis shows it is an equivalent mutant — unreachable-false through the public API. One genuine untested edge exists: a repo whose only remote is non-origin silently changed classification from failure to absence.

## Guard conditions — pinned or not (mutation-verified)

1. **`loadErr == nil` (unreadable settings never classify absence)** — PINNED. Mutation (guard fires on load error) → `UnreadableSettingsNeverClassifiesAbsence` fails.
2. **`!checkpointRemoteKeyPresent(s)` (present-but-malformed key blocks the shortcut)** — PINNED. Mutation (key lookup broken) → `MalformedCheckpointRemoteNeverClassifiesAbsence` fails. Note this test is load-bearing beyond the obvious: `GetCheckpointRemote()` collapses malformed→nil, so only the raw-key check distinguishes this case, and only this test guards that distinction.
3. **`GetRemoteURL(ctx, originRemote)` failing** — NOT pinned (mutation replacing it with `if true` survives the full suite). However, it's provably redundant today: `fetchURLAuthoritative` (`util.go:54-144`) only ever falls back to the literal name `"origin"` when `originURL == ""`, i.e. when `GetRemoteURL(origin)` just failed. Every reachable path into the guard already has no origin. The check is defense-in-depth against future drift in `fetchURLAuthoritative`, and is untestable through the public API without injection. **Severity 2 — acceptable as-is**; the code comment covers the intent. (Same is true of `!authoritative`: the literal-`"origin"` target is never returned as authoritative.)

The guard-must-not-fire-when-origin-exists direction is pinned by the pre-existing `PresentRefFetches` (an over-eager guard would return absence instead of fetching) and `RemoteMissingRefIsAbsence`.

## Missing edge cases

- **Severity 6 — repo whose only remote is non-origin (e.g. `git clone -o upstream`), no checkpoint_remote.** Untested, and it's the one input class where this PR genuinely changed behavior beyond the remoteless case: before, `ls-remote origin` failed with exit 128 (failure, backfill retries); now the guard classifies ABSENCE (`GetRemoteURL(origin)` fails, key absent). This is not obviously wrong — the fetch universe is only origin/checkpoint_remote — but the push side is not so restricted: `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` (`cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:326`) pushes checkpoint refs toward whatever remote the pre-push hook fires for, so refs can exist on a non-origin remote the probe will now call "absent", and absence is a signal write routing acts on. ## What

Restores the git-refs-primary → v1-branch checkpoint fallback that is currently RED on `main` (blocks every PR):

`TestRunExplainAuto_GeneratePersistsHexOnBranchUnderRefsPrimary` fails with
`failed to save summary: fetch checkpoint ref ...: probe checkpoint ref ... on ://origin: git ls-remote: exit status 128`.

## Why

Under a git-refs primary, saving a summary for a pre-migration checkpoint that lives only on the v1 branch resolves the checkpoint through the git-refs store, which triggers an on-demand fetch of the missing ref. When the repo has **no origin remote and no configured `checkpoint_remote`**, fetch-target resolution falls back to the bare `"origin"` name, `git ls-remote origin` fails (exit 128), and `FetchCheckpointRef` returned that as a **hard error**.

Done — the consolidated review fix is pushed to #1886 (`e9fb3e5aaa`). Now your two questions:

## Is the failure hitting anyone else?

**Your hypothesis is exactly right.** CI runs on head SHAs, so only branches whose history *contains* main's tip fail. Survey of recent PRs:

- **#1880–1883** (created before the 14:42 UTC #1811 merge): `test-core` **passes** on all of them — their branches simply don't contain broken main yet.
- **#1885** (mine, cut *from* the broken tip): fails.
- And the strongest signal: **someone else already hit it hard enough to write a fix** — see below.

So the blast radius today is "anyone who branches from or merges current main," which silently becomes *everyone* over the next day as PRs update. Nobody else is red *yet* purely by timing.

## The bigger finding: #1888 is a competing fix for the same bug

`suhaanthayyil` opened **#1888** 47 minutes after my #1886, fixing the identical failure at the identical spot (`FetchCheckpointRef`). Having just run five review agents over this exact code, I can compare precisely:

- **#1888's architecture is better than mine**: it threads a `resolved` flag out of `checkpointFetchTarget` — single source of truth, no re-derived state, which is literally what my reviewers recommended as the ideal shape.
- **But #1888's classification predicate has all four holes my review swarm just made me fix**: it classifies absence whenever resolution produced nothing *and* the probe failed — which is true for **unreadable settings** (their comment even lists it as a qualifying case), **malformed checkpoint_remote**, **a repo whose only remote is `upstream`**, and **a canceled context**. Each is a false "checkpoint doesn't exist" verdict that write routing acts on — the data-fork the function's own contract forbids. My #1886 now requires positive evidence for each of those (readable config, no key at all, confirmed-empty `git remote` listing, live context), with regression tests pinning every one.

The genuinely best fix is **#1888's plumbing + #1886's predicate**. Since coordinating with another author is yours to do, here's a paste-able comment for #1888 if you want it:

> Thanks for jumping on this — same root cause as #1886, and your `resolved` threading is cleaner than the guard over there. One concern before this lands: `!resolved && probe failed` classifies absence for unreadable settings, malformed `checkpoint_remote`, repos whose only remote isn't origin, and canceled contexts — each a false "absent" that write routing acts on. #1886 has regression tests for all four (they'd fail against this branch). Maybe combine: your resolver flag + the positive-evidence checks (readable config with no checkpoint_remote key, confirmed-empty `git remote` listing, `ctx.Err() == nil`)?

Either PR can absorb the other; the tests in #1886 are the part I'd insist survives regardless of whose code wins.

24	
25	The visible CLI is organized around a set of noun groups plus a small set of
26	top-level verbs. The groups are the canonical home for each verb; legacy
27	top-level shortcuts remain functional but hidden, and emit a deprecation hint
28	pointing at the canonical group form. Newer experimental command families are

31	
32	Experimental commands are gated by a build-time visibility flag (the
33	`cmd/entire/cli/experimental` package): they are shown — grouped under an
34	"Experimental commands:" help section — in developer and nightly builds, and
35	hidden in stable release builds. Visibility is toggled by `experimental.Visible`
36	(default `"true"`), which GoReleaser stamps `"false"` only on stable tags
37	(`.Prerelease` empty); nightly (`vX.Y.Z-nightly.*`) and local builds leave it at
38	the default. Register a command as experimental with `experimental.Register(parent,
39	child)` instead of `parent.AddCommand(child)`. Gating only controls visibility —
40	the commands are always runnable in every build.

42	- `session` (alias: `sessions`): `list`, `info`, `tokens`, `stop`, `attach`, `adopt`, `resume`, `current`.
43	  `resume` with a branch arg switches to it and resumes its session; with no arg
44	  it opens an interactive picker of stopped sessions (across all worktrees),
45	  resolving each to its branch and pointing at the owning worktree when the
46	  branch is checked out elsewhere. Resume keeps an existing local session log
47	  as-is by default (`--force` overwrites it from the checkpoint).
48	  `adopt` moves an active session from another repo or worktree into the current
49	  worktree and resets target-local checkpoint bookkeeping so future commits link
50	  to the adopted session from the new location.
51	- `checkpoint` (aliases: `cp`, `checkpoints`): `list`, `explain`, `tokens`, `search`, plus

56	  manage non-agent settings (telemetry, git-hook installation mode, strategy
57	  options, summary provider). Agent CRUD lives under `entire agent`.
58	- `auth`: `login`, `logout`, `status`, `contexts`, `use`, plus
59	  `token` (prints the active control-plane bearer to stdout for scripting/curl;
60	  honors `ENTIRE_TOKEN`, else the refreshed active-context login JWT). `token`

76	- `grant`: manage access grants and org membership — `org`, `project`, and `repo`
